title: Dubhghall drives the gully alone for the first time
summary: At twenty-five, Dubhghall stands for the first time at the head of the deer-drive he has watched his uncle lead since boyhood, and takes a stag with a bad throw that his uncle and two others must finish for him, a failure the household forgets within the season.

title: The stand of antlers grows at the gully's mouth
summary: Two autumns running, a good drive leaves the stacked antlers at the mouth of the glen tall enough for a boy to stand in their shadow at noon, the household's plain mark of what the year's meat has cost the herd.

title: Dubhghall's uncle dies
summary: Worn thin by winters and no longer able to stand a whole autumn morning at the gully, Dubhghall's uncle dies and is buried within sight of the glen's mouth, close enough that his grandchildren can point to the rise from the stand of horn.

title: Dubhghall's grandson's dog dies
summary: A dog that has slept across the boy's feet every night since it was weaned lies down by the hearth one evening and does not rise the next morning, found stiff and cold before the household is properly awake.

title: The boy digs the dog a grave and sets a shell at its head
summary: On the dry rise above the house, the boy digs a grave the length of a dog, lays it on its side as a sleeping dog lies, and sets at its head a sea-shell kept idle on a hearth-shelf for years, telling no one beforehand and asking no leave.

title: An old woman questions the dog's grave
summary: At a gathering of the near hearths an older woman asks the boy, not unkindly, whether he means to give every lost lamb a shell as well; he answers only that the dog slept at his feet for nine years and a lamb never did, and she allows it is answer enough.

title: Two more households bury dogs at Cnoc fhionn
summary: Within a few years of the first grave, two neighbouring households bury their own dogs the same way, a shell at the head and a proper grave dug, and the custom begins to travel hearth to hearth through the hill country.

title: Dubhghall dies at Cnoc fhionn
summary: Dubhghall dies in his sixty-fifth year among his daughter's family, remembered at his own leaving for thirty autumns of driving the glen without losing a man to horn or wet ground; his grandson sets the last of his kept shells at the old man's head.

title: The young man of the northern moor builds a boat for Eilean ghorm
summary: In a season of want, a young man of the northern moor spends a hard winter building a hide boat in secret and puts out alone one grey morning for the geese's island, telling no one what the boat is for.

title: The young man does not come back a hunter
summary: What became of the young man who sailed for Eilean ghorm is told three ways at three hearths and agreed by none of them; he is remembered after not as one who found good hunting, but as a warning the country keeps without understanding it.

title: Dubhghall's grandson asks why no one hunts the geese
summary: Watching the grey line come in over the water one still evening, the boy asks his grandfather why no household takes the geese of Eilean ghorm for meat; Dubhghall answers only that a people who stop leaving what they have always left are no longer quite the people they were.

title: A boy of the northern moor sights Skell
summary: Following a fox further than he has ever gone, a boy of the northern moor lies hidden above the coast-people's greatest landing and watches hulls, smoke and moving people beyond counting until the light fails, then carries the sight home whole.

title: The boy's telling of Skell travels unshrunk
summary: Carried hearth to hearth, the boy's account of the crowded shore loses nothing in the telling, for there is nothing in it that wants adding to; no one presses him for who the coast-people are or whence they came, an answer his own eyes never gave him.

title: The mole at Skell stands two hundred years and more
summary: Mended and lengthened season on season since its first builders, the mole at the coast-people's western landing runs further into the river's mouth than any one lifetime could have raised, sheltering more boats at once than a hunter of the moor has words to count.
